The Value of Information

Should you invest or not? A signal helps you decide. The more accurate the signal, the better the decision. After seeing the signal, you recompute the probability. A good signal says invest. A bad signal says stop. The value of information is the gap between deciding with it and without it. The formula below pins that gap down. For example, before buying a used 🚗 car, you ask an expert. The expert spots good and bad cars correctly 80 percent of the time. If the expert says good, you buy. If the expert says bad, you walk away. Your losses shrink a lot.

P(good∣h)=πqπq+(1−π)(1−q)P(\text{good} \mid h) = \frac{\pi q}{\pi q + (1-\pi)(1-q)}P(good∣h)=πq+(1−π)(1−q)πq​
VoI=P(h)max⁡(0,EVh)+P(l)max⁡(0,EVl)−max⁡(0,πR−(1−π)L)\text{VoI} = P(h)\max(0, \text{EV}_h) + P(l)\max(0, \text{EV}_l) - \max(0, \pi R - (1-\pi)L)VoI=P(h)max(0,EVh​)+P(l)max(0,EVl​)−max(0,πR−(1−π)L)

After hhh, 0.8⋅100−0.2⋅60=68>00.8 \cdot 100 - 0.2 \cdot 60 = 68 > 00.8⋅100−0.2⋅60=68>0, so invest; after lll, 0.2⋅100−0.8⋅60=−28<00.2 \cdot 100 - 0.8 \cdot 60 = -28 < 00.2⋅100−0.8⋅60=−28<0, so stay out. With P(h)=0.5P(h) = 0.5P(h)=0.5, EVwith=0.5⋅68+0.5⋅0=34\text{EV}_{\text{with}} = 0.5 \cdot 68 + 0.5 \cdot 0 = 34EVwith​=0.5⋅68+0.5⋅0=34.
